summary:
Mali's Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code on 31 October 2024. It was promulgated in December 2024 and took effect on 13 December 2024, published in Official Journal Special No. 21 of 2024. The code defines homosexuality as sexual relations between persons of the same sex and punishes it with two to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 200,000 to 500,000 CFA francs. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 6 November 2024, describes the penalties as harsh.

The code recognises no affirmed gender. The offence is fixed by sex assigned at birth, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local authorities would class as same-sex under birth-registered status falls inside its terms, and a traveller whose presentation is read as gender-nonconforming can be arrested on perceived same-sex conduct.

The statute also bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality and reaches any citizen seen to encourage it. Because the term is left undefined, the provision covers people well beyond those accused of conduct itself, and Human Rights Watch states the drafting is broad enough for expansive application.

Before the code took effect, same-sex conduct was not explicitly criminalised in Mali, but the vague public indecency provisions of Article 225 were already used against LGBT people and against gender-nonconforming expression, and laws against attacks on morality were actively enforced against the same groups. That enforcement record predates the criminalisation now in force and indicates how the new provisions are likely to be applied.

Since the code came into effect, reporting records a significant increase in arbitrary arrests and detentions, and in physical abuse directed at individuals on the basis of appearance or gender expression alone.

No anti-discrimination law protects against harassment or abuse on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so neither a visitor nor a resident has a domestic complaint mechanism or protection body to invoke.

The constitution adopted by referendum in June 2023 limits marriage to a union of one man and one woman, which closes partner recognition in Mali for a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law.
tangentialFactors:
The criminalisation arrived alongside wider repression. The military junta ruling since 2021 has moved against opposition and media, and it justified the penal code as a defence of traditional and moral values. Justice Minister Mamadou Kassogue had earlier described homosexuality as unnatural and pledged to criminalise it.

US State Department human-rights reporting for 2021 recorded that same-sex conduct was not criminalised at that time, that societal stigma was significant, and that violence and instability caused by armed groups formed a parallel human-rights problem. The department's 2011 report had already listed discrimination based on sexual orientation among the country's human-rights problems, alongside gender inequality, female genital mutilation and corruption.
localsOnly:
Article 522 of the Code des Personnes et de la Famille, passed by the National Assembly on 2 December 2011 and signed by the president, forbids same-sex couples from adopting children.

Organised advocacy has no legal footing. A law prohibiting association for an immoral purpose was cited in 2005 to refuse recognition to a gay rights association in Bamako, and the 2011 human-rights findings recorded no publicly visible lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender organisations in the country. The same provision is described as continuing to impede free association.

A 2007 survey found 98 percent of Malian adults believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and a health provider director, Dr. Dembelé Bintou Keita, described Malian society as not tolerant of men who have sex with men, adding that all cultural beliefs towards them are negative.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Mali could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403). That organisation's profile documents the new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 chapter on Mali, covering events of 2024, contains no transgender-specific content and no information on prison placement, special units, or solitary confinement and segregation practice for transgender prisoners. Its coverage of the junta's rule, counterterrorism sweeps and an international arrest warrant carries no transgender dimension.

No source in hand states a documented position on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the attitude data available addresses homosexuality and men who have sex with men.

The reported increase in arbitrary arrests and physical abuse since December 2024 is described qualitatively. No count, rate or comparison with general detention figures is provided, so its scale is unresolved.

No entry rule, visa provision, screening practice or identity-document requirement specific to transgender travellers is documented in the sources consulted.
